implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: start from a general n-ary function, fix its configuration arguments into a new function value with a binder (closure, partial object, method value or placeholder expression), and let consumers advertise only the remaining arity; the curried variant goes further and restates the function as unary steps, so that application itself becomes composition. Keep the bound values immutable, name each specialisation where it is created, and hoist construction out of loops and request handlers - a specialisation built per iteration is the most common way to turn a free abstraction into an allocation and an extra call frame per element. Where the language has dedicated primitives (bind, curry, partial, method values) prefer those for better introspection, signature metadata or framework integration; use a plain closure when type inference or extra logic matters more.
code_sketch:
bind(general, bound...) -> function of the remaining parameters

add5       = bind(add, 5)                        # partial application: 5 is fixed
chain      = curry(add3)                         # currying: add3(x)(y)(z)
format_eur = bind(format, currency="EUR", locale="de-DE")
register('/orders', bind(handle_orders, repo))   # only the request remains
pitfalls: Binding the leading parameters makes the general function's parameter order part of every specialisation; when configuration is not first, the binder is an argument flip in disguise.
Every specialisation is a closure or partial object: created per call it allocates, and created over mutable state it silently shares that state.
Currying and partial application are not interchangeable: a curried function demands one argument per call, so a consumer expecting the remaining arity receives a function instead of a value.

Auto-curry implementations that use fn.length miscount when functions have default parameters or rest parameters; pass arity explicitly (e.g. curryN arity, fn.length is unreliable for parameterised signatures).
Over-currying: a chain like f(a)(b)(c)(d) is harder to read than a single named call; use it when it genuinely removes repetition, not as a default style.
Stack traces lose the domain name: a specialised function is anonymous, so profiler output and error messages show 'bound <name>' rather than the semantic role of the function.

Wrong move: reaching for C++ std::bind to partially apply a function or member call -> failure: std::bind is not straightforward partial application — every argument must be spelled out with a placeholder, unreferenced arguments are silently dropped, and the opaque result type breaks compile-time checks like std::is_invocable -> instead: use a lambda, or std::bind_front/absl::bind_front, which bind only the leading arguments (Abseil TotW #108, P0356).

Wrong move: declaring multi-parameter-list curried functions in Swift (func f(x: Int)(y: Int)) -> failure: Swift 3 removed the syntax (SE-0002) because currying's marginal utility did not justify the grammar and implementation complexity, so such declarations no longer compile -> instead: return the closure explicitly, func f(x: Int) -> (Int) -> Int.

Wrong move: leaning on Scala's underscore placeholder for partial application (list map f(_)) -> failure: the placeholder-syntax form of partial application was dropped in Scala 3.0, so code written against it breaks on migration -> instead: write the lambda (x => f(x)) or rely on universal eta-expansion (map(f)).
